subsection: 1. The rock cycle and rock formation

notes.h: The rock cycle: forces that form, modify, destroy and reconstitute rock
notes.b: Rock is never permanent. It is continually formed, modified, destroyed and reconstituted (built again from the broken pieces), so the three rock types are linked in one cycle. Two sets of forces drive it, one working from inside the earth and one at its surface.
points: Endogenic (internal) forces, driven from within the earth, form and modify rock through magma (molten rock below the surface), heat and pressure.
Exogenic (external) forces, working at the surface, destroy rock through weathering (breakdown of rock in place by weather) and erosion (wearing away and carrying off of rock fragments).
Deposition (dropping of carried sediment, the loose fragments of rock) reconstitutes rock, because the sediment is later turned into new sedimentary rock.
notes.tip: A past question type is to label a rock cycle diagram, so know which force goes with which job: endogenic forms and modifies, exogenic destroys, deposition reconstitutes.

notes.h: The rock cycle as a diagram
notes.b: The cycle is easiest to learn as a circular flow chart in which each rock type is reached from another by a named process. Short-cuts across the circle show that rock does not have to follow the full loop.
points: 1. Magma cools and crystallises (forms crystals as it hardens) to make igneous rock.
2. Weathering and erosion break igneous rock down into sediment, because rock at the surface is attacked by weather.
3. Deposition, compaction and cementation turn the sediment into sedimentary rock, because the layers are squeezed and glued together.
4. Heat and pressure change sedimentary rock into metamorphic rock, because buried rock is squeezed and heated without melting.
5. Melting turns the metamorphic rock back into magma, and the cycle starts again.
Short-cuts: any rock can be weathered into sediment, and any rock can be metamorphosed (changed by heat and pressure) or melted, so the arrows do not all follow one loop.
Diagram: draw a circular flow chart with magma and the three rock types as the nodes, and label each arrow with its process, for example crystallisation or compaction and cementation.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to label the stages and the processes: crystallisation of magma, weathering and erosion, compaction and cementation, and heat and pressure.

notes.h: The rock cycle and plate tectonics
notes.b: The rock cycle does not run at random. It is tied to the moving plates (the large slabs that make up the earth's crust), which decide where each stage happens.
points: Rock is created at plate boundaries and at hotspots (fixed points of rising magma), because magma reaches the crust there.
Rock is metamorphosed at collision zones, where plates push together and the heat and pressure are great.
Rock is destroyed or recycled at subduction zones, where one plate sinks beneath another and the rock melts back into magma.

notes.h: Igneous rock: how it forms and why crystal size varies
notes.b: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and crystallises. Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is molten rock at the surface. Where the rock cools decides how big its crystals grow.
points: Crystal size depends on cooling rate: slow cooling gives large crystals because they have time to grow, and fast cooling gives small ones.
Plutonic (intrusive) rock is igneous rock that cools slowly deep in the crust, so its crystals are large.
Volcanic (extrusive) rock is lava that cools quickly at the surface, so its crystals are small.
Uses: granite is used as building stone, kerbs, worktops and headstones; basalt is crushed for road chippings and aggregate (crushed stone used in construction).
notes.tip: Define plutonic rock on its own, as slowly cooled igneous rock deep in the crust with large crystals. You may also be asked for two uses of rock.

notes.b: Granite is a plutonic rock. When magma pushes into surrounding rock and cools there, it forms masses called intrusions, and their shape gives them different names.
points: Granite is a plutonic rock built from quartz, feldspar and mica crystals, which are large enough to see because the magma cooled slowly.
Batholiths are huge dome-shaped masses of plutonic rock.
Dykes are vertical intrusions that cut across the beds (layers) of the rock around them.
Sills are horizontal intrusions that lie along bedding planes (the horizontal surfaces between layers).
Plutonic rock reaches the surface only after the rock above it has been eroded away, because it formed deep underground.
notes.tip: Basalt is volcanic (extrusive), not plutonic, and granite is igneous, not sedimentary. Both come up as true/false items.

notes.h: Volcanic rock and where igneous rock forms
notes.b: Volcanic rock forms at the surface, so it cools fast. Which kind forms depends on the plate setting, the tectonic setting, in which the magma reaches the crust.
points: Basalt is the commonest volcanic rock and forms from runny lava, which flows easily before it sets.
Basalt forms at constructive (divergent) boundaries, where plates move apart, and at hotspots.
Andesite and granite batholiths form above subduction zones at destructive boundaries, where one plate sinks beneath another.

notes.b: Sedimentary rock is formed from sediment laid down in layers (strata), usually in seas, lakes, river basins and deserts. Loose sediment then has to be turned into solid rock.
points: Sediment comes from weathered and eroded fragments of older rock, from the remains of plants and animals, or from minerals precipitated from water (that is, coming out of solution as solids).

Sediment builds up in subsiding basins (areas of sinking land), on continental shelves (the shallow sea floor around a continent) and along trailing (passive) margins, where no plate boundary lies at the coast.
Lithification is the conversion of loose sediment into solid rock by compaction and cementation.
Compaction: the weight of overlying layers squeezes out water and air, packing the grains together.
Cementation: minerals such as silica, calcite and iron oxide, carried by groundwater, bind the grains together like glue.
notes.tip: Define lithification on its own: loose sediment turned to solid rock by compaction and cementation. Silica can bind sedimentary particles, which is true.

notes.b: Because sedimentary rock is laid down in layers from material at the earth's surface, it often contains fossils and shows bedding planes.
points: Many sedimentary rocks contain fossils, the remains or traces of past life, because living things were buried in the sediment.
Bedding planes are horizontal surfaces separating one layer from the next.
Joints are vertical cracks that cut through the layers.
Many sedimentary rocks are porous, holding water in the spaces between grains. Porous is not the same as permeable (letting water pass through).
notes.tip: Fossils occur in sedimentary rock: that statement is true. Granite being sedimentary is false.

notes.b: Sedimentary rocks are sorted into three groups by the material they are made from.
points: Clastic rocks are made of broken fragments: sandstone from sand, and shale from mud and clay.
Organic rocks are made of the remains of living things: limestone from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures, and coal from plant remains that accumulated in swamps.
Chemical rocks form from minerals that come out of solution: rock salt and other evaporites form as seawater evaporates and leaves its dissolved minerals behind.
notes.tip: Know the source material: limestone from shells and skeletons of sea creatures, sandstone from sand.

notes.h: Irish sedimentary rocks and the conditions of their formation
notes.b: Each Irish sedimentary rock records the conditions in which it formed, such as the climate and the setting at that time. For a longer answer, give the conditions as well as the rock and its place.
points: Carboniferous limestone (Carboniferous period, about 360 to 300 million years ago) formed when Ireland lay near the equator under a warm, shallow, clear sea, where shells and skeletons built up the deposit. It covers most of the central lowland and forms the Burren, Co. Clare.
Old Red Sandstone (Devonian period) formed in hot, semi-arid (very dry) conditions from sand and pebbles laid down by rivers; its red colour comes from iron oxide.
Old Red Sandstone forms the Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtees and the Comeraghs.
Shale and sandstone of the Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare, are layers of shale, siltstone and sandstone.
Chalk lies beneath the basalt along the Antrim coast, so the chalk is the older rock and the lava flowed over it.
Coal at Arigna, Co. Roscommon, and Castlecomer, Co. Kilkenny, formed from plant remains in swamps; both are former coal-mining areas.
Rock salt is mined at the Kilroot salt mine, near Carrickfergus, Co. Antrim.
notes.tip: A Higher Level question asks for the formation of sedimentary rocks with Irish examples. For each rock give where it is and the conditions at the time it formed.

notes.b: Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock is changed by great heat and/or pressure without melting. The original rock is called the parent rock.
points: The two factors that cause metamorphism are heat and pressure.
Minerals recrystallise (re-form as new crystals) while the rock stays solid, so the rock usually becomes harder and denser.
The rock may develop banding or cleavage (a tendency to split along flat surfaces).
notes.tip: Short definitions are asked, so be able to state the two factors that cause metamorphism: heat and pressure.

notes.b: Metamorphism happens on two scales, depending on whether the heat and pressure come from a single intrusion or from the movement of plates.
points: Thermal (contact) metamorphism: rock beside an igneous intrusion is baked by its heat, forming a ring of altered rock called a metamorphic aureole; it is small in scale.
Regional metamorphism: heat and pressure act over huge areas during plate collision and mountain building; it is large in scale.
notes.tip: To tell the two apart in a definition, give the cause (an intrusion's heat or plate collision) and the scale (small or large).

notes.h: Parent rocks and the metamorphic rocks they form
notes.b: Each metamorphic rock comes from a particular parent rock, and the pairs can be asked either way round.
points: Limestone becomes marble; Connemara marble is green and is quarried in Connemara, Co. Galway.
Sandstone becomes quartzite, so the parent of quartzite is a sedimentary rock.
Shale (mudstone) becomes slate, and with more heat and pressure becomes schist, so schist is the more strongly altered rock. Slate is quarried on Valentia Island, Co. Kerry.
Granite becomes gneiss, so gneiss is a metamorphic rock formed from an igneous parent.
Quartzite forms Errigal, Co. Donegal; Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo; the Great Sugar Loaf, Co. Wicklow; and the Twelve Bens, Connemara.
Mica schist is found in Donegal and Connemara, and a metamorphic aureole of mica schist surrounds the Leinster granite.
Gneiss at Inishtrahull, off Co. Donegal, is about 1.7 billion years old and is the oldest rock in Ireland.
notes.tip: Limestone becomes marble, not quartzite. Croagh Patrick is quartzite, not granite. Only give these parent pairs: schist comes from shale, never from an igneous rock such as basalt.

notes.h: Irish rock types and Ireland's geological past
notes.b: Ireland's rock types form a recognisable pattern across the island, and each reflects an event in its geological past.
points: Limestone floors the central lowland, and Old Red Sandstone forms the ridges of Munster.
Granite outcrops (shows at the surface) in Wicklow, Donegal and the Mournes; basalt covers Co. Antrim; metamorphic rocks lie in Donegal, Connemara and Mayo.
Plutonic example: the Leinster batholith, the granite core of the Wicklow Mountains, is about 400 million years old and is the largest granite mass in Ireland and Britain.
The Mourne granite, in the Mourne Mountains, Co. Down, is much younger, about 56 million years old.
Volcanic example: the Antrim plateau was built by lava flows about 60 million years ago, as the Atlantic began to open. The Giant's Causeway, Co. Antrim, is basalt columns.
The closing of the Iapetus Ocean during Caledonian mountain building produced the Leinster and Donegal granites and regional metamorphism.
notes.tip: Maps of Ireland with lettered locations are used to test rock types, such as limestone, basalt, sandstone and granite. Learn the pattern above. Name an Irish location for each rock you give.

notes.h: North America: active and trailing margins
notes.b: North America has two very different edges. The western edge is an active plate margin, where plates are moving and rock is made and changed. The eastern edge is a trailing (passive) margin, where no plate boundary lies at the coast.
points: Active western margin: Pacific plates subduct (sink) beneath or slide past North America.
Volcanic rock: the Cascade Range volcanoes, including Mount St Helens in Washington state (erupted 1980), lie above a subducting oceanic plate.
Plutonic rock: the Sierra Nevada granite batholith, California.
Regional metamorphism affects the western mountain belts.
The San Andreas Fault, California, is a transform boundary where plates slide past each other.
Trailing eastern margin: there is no plate boundary at the coast, so there are no active volcanoes.
Because the margin is quiet, thick sediments accumulate on the Atlantic coastal plain, on the continental shelf and in the Mississippi delta.
The Appalachians are old, worn-down fold mountains of sedimentary and metamorphic rock.

notes.b: Rocks can be told apart by what they look like, and photo questions rely on this. Each rock below has one or two clues that separate it from the others.
points: Granite: speckled, with large interlocking crystals, because it cooled slowly underground.
Basalt: dark and fine-grained because it cooled quickly; it may form columns, as at the Giant's Causeway.
Sandstone: gritty grains, often reddish or buff, and layered, because it is made of cemented sand laid down in beds.
Limestone: pale grey, and it may show fossils because it is made from shells and skeletons.
Marble: white or coloured, with sparkling crystals and no fossils, which separates it from limestone, its parent rock.
Quartzite: pale, very hard and glassy.
Slate: dark grey, and it splits into thin sheets, which is the cleavage (splitting) that metamorphism can produce.
notes.tip: Photos of granite, basalt, sandstone, limestone, marble, slate and quartzite are to be matched to names and classed as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic. Marble is metamorphic.

keyTerms.definition: Forces from within the earth that form and modify rock through magma, heat and pressure.
Forces acting at the earth's surface, such as weathering and erosion, that destroy rock.
Molten rock below the earth's surface.
Molten rock that has reached the earth's surface.
Igneous rock formed by slow cooling deep in the crust, with large crystals.
Igneous rock formed by the rapid cooling of lava at the surface, with small crystals.
A huge dome-shaped mass of plutonic rock.
A horizontal surface that separates one sedimentary layer from the next.
The conversion of loose sediment into solid sedimentary rock by compaction and cementation.
The squeezing out of water and air from sediment by the weight of overlying layers.
The binding of sediment grains by minerals carried in groundwater.
Metamorphism caused by the heat of an igneous intrusion, forming a small-scale metamorphic aureole.
Metamorphism caused by heat and pressure over large areas during plate collision and mountain building.
A ring of altered rock surrounding an igneous intrusion.

factCards.term: Rock cycle: the processes that link the three rock types
factCards.definition: Magma crystallises into igneous rock; weathering and erosion make sediment; deposition, compaction and cementation make sedimentary rock; heat and pressure make metamorphic rock; melting makes magma again. Any rock can be weathered, metamorphosed or melted.

factCards.term: Plate settings: where igneous rocks form and where rock is recycled
factCards.definition: Basalt forms at constructive (divergent) boundaries and hotspots; andesite and granite batholiths form above subduction zones at destructive boundaries. Rock is metamorphosed at collision zones and destroyed or recycled at subduction zones.

factCards.term: Irish granite: three locations, and the ages of two
factCards.definition: The Leinster batholith, the granite core of the Wicklow Mountains, about 400 million years old and the largest granite mass in Ireland and Britain; the Derryveagh Mountains, Donegal; the Mourne Mountains, Co. Down, much younger at about 56 million years.

factCards.term: Irish basalt: where it is found and how it formed
factCards.definition: The Antrim plateau, Co. Antrim, was built by lava flows about 60 million years ago as the Atlantic began to open; the Giant's Causeway shows basalt columns. Basalt forms when runny lava cools quickly, so its crystals are small.

factCards.term: Rock uses: what granite and basalt are used for
factCards.definition: Granite: building stone, kerbs, worktops and headstones. Basalt: crushed for road chippings and aggregate.

factCards.term: Sedimentary rock: how it forms, from weathering to solid rock
factCards.definition: Older rock is weathered and eroded; the sediment, plant and animal remains, or minerals from water are laid down in layers in seas, lakes, river basins or deserts; compaction squeezes out water and air; silica, calcite or iron oxide cement the grains.

factCards.term: Sedimentary rock: three groups, with examples of each
factCards.definition: Clastic, from broken fragments: sandstone from sand, shale from mud and clay. Organic, from living things: limestone from shells and skeletons of sea creatures, coal from swamp plants. Chemical: rock salt and other evaporites from evaporating seawater.

factCards.term: Carboniferous limestone: when and how it formed, and where it is found
factCards.definition: About 360 to 300 million years ago Ireland lay near the equator under a warm, shallow, clear sea, where shells and skeletons built up the deposit. It floors most of the central lowland and forms the Burren, Co. Clare.

factCards.term: Old Red Sandstone: how it formed, and three places it forms mountains
factCards.definition: In the Devonian period, in hot, semi-arid conditions, rivers laid down sand and pebbles; iron oxide gives the red colour. It forms the Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtees and the Comeraghs, and the ridges of Munster.

factCards.term: Name Irish locations for shale, chalk, coal and rock salt
factCards.definition: Shale, with siltstone and sandstone: the Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare. Chalk: beneath the basalt along the Antrim coast. Coal, from swamp plants: Arigna, Co. Roscommon, and Castlecomer, Co. Kilkenny. Rock salt: Kilroot mine, near Carrickfergus, Co. Antrim.

factCards.term: Metamorphism: what heat and pressure do to a rock
factCards.definition: Existing rock is changed without melting: its minerals recrystallise while it stays solid, so it usually becomes harder and denser, and it may develop banding or cleavage. The two causes are heat and pressure.

factCards.term: Name the metamorphic rock formed from limestone, sandstone, shale and granite
factCards.definition: Limestone becomes marble; sandstone becomes quartzite; shale (mudstone) becomes slate, and with more heat and pressure schist; granite becomes gneiss.

factCards.term: Name Irish locations for marble, quartzite and slate
factCards.definition: Marble: green Connemara marble, Co. Galway. Quartzite: Errigal, Co. Donegal; Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo; the Great Sugar Loaf, Co. Wicklow; the Twelve Bens, Connemara. Slate: Valentia Island, Co. Kerry.

factCards.term: Schist and gneiss: where they are found in Ireland
factCards.definition: Mica schist occurs in Donegal and Connemara, and as a metamorphic aureole around the Leinster granite. Gneiss on Inishtrahull, off Co. Donegal, is about 1.7 billion years old, the oldest rock in Ireland.

factCards.term: Map of Ireland: where each main rock type is found
factCards.definition: Limestone floors the central lowland; Old Red Sandstone forms the ridges of Munster; granite in Wicklow, Donegal and the Mournes; basalt in Co. Antrim; metamorphic rocks in Donegal, Connemara and Mayo.

factCards.term: North America's active western margin: rocks and features formed
factCards.definition: Pacific plates subduct beneath it or slide past it. Volcanic: Cascade volcanoes, e.g. Mount St Helens (erupted 1980). Plutonic: the Sierra Nevada batholith. Regional metamorphism: western mountain belts. Transform boundary: the San Andreas Fault, California.

factCards.term: North America's trailing eastern margin: what forms there
factCards.definition: No plate boundary at the coast, so no active volcanoes. Thick sediments build up on the Atlantic coastal plain, on the continental shelf and in the Mississippi delta. The Appalachians are old, worn-down fold mountains of sedimentary and metamorphic rock.

factCards.term: Photo skill: how to identify granite, basalt, sandstone and limestone
factCards.definition: Granite: speckled, with large interlocking crystals. Basalt: dark and fine-grained, and may form columns. Sandstone: gritty grains, often reddish or buff, and layered. Limestone: pale grey, and may show fossils.

factCards.term: Photo skill: how to identify marble, quartzite and slate
factCards.definition: Marble: white or coloured, with sparkling crystals and no fossils. Quartzite: pale, very hard and glassy. Slate: dark grey, and splits into thin sheets.

questions.prompt: Examine the formation of sedimentary rocks, with reference to Irish examples.
questions.model: Sedimentary rocks form from sediment, which comes from weathered and eroded fragments of older rock, from the remains of plants and animals, or from minerals precipitated from water. Weathering breaks the older rock down, erosion removes the fragments, and deposition lays them down in layers (strata) in seas, lakes, river basins and deserts, usually in subsiding basins. Sediment builds up in layers that are separated by bedding planes. Lithification turns the loose sediment into solid rock in two stages. Compaction: the weight of the overlying layers squeezes out water and air and packs the grains together. Cementation: minerals such as silica, calcite and iron oxide, carried by groundwater, bind the grains together. Organic rocks form from the remains of living things. Carboniferous limestone formed in the Carboniferous period, about 360 to 300 million years ago, when Ireland lay near the equator under a warm, shallow, clear sea; shells and skeletons of sea creatures built up the deposit, and it covers most of the central lowland. Old Red Sandstone formed in the Devonian period in hot, semi-arid conditions, when rivers laid down sand and pebbles; iron oxide gives it its red colour, and it forms the ridges of Munster. Shale and sandstone at the Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare, are layers of shale, siltstone and sandstone. Coal at Arigna, Co. Roscommon, and Castlecomer, Co. Kilkenny, formed from plant remains that accumulated in swamps. Clastic rocks form from broken fragments: sandstone from sand and shale from mud and clay. Chemical rocks form from minerals that come out of solution: rock salt at Kilroot, near Carrickfergus, Co. Antrim, was deposited as seawater evaporated.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain how igneous rocks are formed. Name one igneous rock and a location where it is found.
questions.model: Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools and crystallises. Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is molten rock at the surface. The rate of cooling controls crystal size: slow cooling gives large crystals and fast cooling gives small crystals. Plutonic rocks form when magma cools slowly deep in the crust, so the crystals grow large. Magma can form batholiths, dykes and sills before it reaches the surface, and plutonic rock is exposed only after the rock above it has been eroded away. Granite is a plutonic rock; the Leinster batholith, the granite core of the Wicklow Mountains, is about 400 million years old. Volcanic rocks form when lava cools quickly at the surface, so the crystals are small. Basalt is the commonest volcanic rock and forms from runny lava, at constructive boundaries and hotspots; the basalt of the Antrim plateau was formed by lava flows about 60 million years ago. Andesite and granite batholiths form above subduction zones at destructive plate boundaries.

questions.prompt: Explain briefly how rocks are changed by thermal metamorphism and by regional metamorphism.
questions.model: Thermal (contact) metamorphism happens when rock beside an igneous intrusion is baked by its heat. The altered rock forms a small-scale ring called a metamorphic aureole; for example, limestone changes to marble. Regional metamorphism happens when heat and pressure act over huge areas during plate collision and mountain building. The rock recrystallises while still solid, becoming harder and denser; for example, sandstone changes to quartzite.
